newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury drops two 10-year note sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury drops two 10-year note sales.

text.p: The Treasury Department announced on Monday that it was scrapping sales of conventional 10-year notes in July and October and introducing a new five-year inflation-protected security.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Treasury was able to eliminate two of six annual sales of fixed-rate 10-year notes because of progress in cutting the government's budget deficit and the success of inflation-indexed securities that it began selling last January.
"We have been pleased with the market response (to the 10-year indexed notes)," Summers told a news conference. "A liquid market has developed."

Treasury plans to expand its offerings of inflation-protected securities in several stages, starting with a new five-year maturity to be auctioned next month. It expects to reopen that issue at an auction in October.
A new 10-year indexed note will be sold next January, Summers said. Sometime next year, Treasury also will begin offering inflation-indexed bonds with a 30-year maturity.
"By the end of next year, we expect to establish a regular schedule for offering inflation-indexed securities with maturities of five, 10 and 30 years," Summers said.
Over time, Treasury expects to increase the proportion of government debt issued in the form of inflation-protected securities to "a substantial fraction," Summers said.
He declined to specify how frequently sales of five, 10 and 30-year indexed securities will occur. "We'll have to see," he said in response to questions.
Summers repeated, in response to questions, that Treasury plans to also offer an inflation-protected U.S. Savings Bond early next year.

Some analysts have said the inflation-protected securities might be less attractive to investors because inflation has been low and stable. Summers acknowledged that inflation was remaining under control but nonetheless extolled the benefits of the new securities, saying they have been "less volatile" than conventional securities, partly because of changed inflation expectations.
Summers was noncommital when asked whether Treasury might be able to scrap more sales of conventional 10-year notes in addition to the two sales that it is dropping in July and October.
